primary_text:
Week 10, Tuesday, 9:40pm. I changed the theme image on my store again. That's the fourth one, and the store still isn't live.

Tonight I pressed the go-live button one more time. "Something went wrong." It won't let me get on live at all, and nothing on the screen says why.

I want to be clear about one thing, because I know how this sounds. I'm tech savvy and competent. I run the front desk at a dental office. I cannot find a simple step by step for this.

Ten weeks on simple tasks.

My sister thinks the store is almost done. I've been saying "almost done" since week four.

What scares me isn't the money. It's becoming the person who built a whole store and never launched it.

I didn't know yet that a woman I'd never met, standing by a cooler at my nephew's birthday party, was about to tell me I'd been asking the wrong question the whole time.

I should back up. I kept notes on my phone the whole way through. Here they are, mostly the way I wrote them.

Week 1, Sunday. Opened the account. Picked a theme. Bought a domain the same night. Figured I'd be live by Friday. Normal people set up stores all the time, right?

Week 2, Monday. First monthly charge for the plan. Zero products listed, and I'm already paying for it.

Week 3, Thursday. Third night in the help pages. Tons of links, like a snowstorm of information, but nothing that actually helps me! Just performing one task is a marathon of reading.

Week 4. Tried the chat. Then the bot. Then email. The bot sent me the same article three times. Never an answer to the basic question, which was how to put my own photo on the front page.

Week 5, Saturday. It's asking me for my first product. Do I just choose what I want to sell? Candles on Monday. Dog bandanas by Wednesday. Phone stands on Friday. I have a spreadsheet full of product ideas and zero products. I keep jumping from one idea to another.

Week 6, Friday. Skipped dinner with my friends to fight the shipping settings. Told them I had a migraine. What I actually had was a shipping profile that wouldn't save. Got stuck four times on one page.

Week 7. Cancelled the whole thing and started over. Second attempt, same spot. Now I'm eyeing a different platform, which I know is just starting over with extra steps.

Week 8. YouTube on my lunch break, YouTube at 11pm with my tea going cold by the trackpad and my eyes burning. I watched one nine-minute video three times for a thirty-second answer. The one thing in the video never looks like the one thing on my screen. It's intensely time consuming and aggravating.

Week 9, Wednesday. Opened a tab to pay somebody to build it. Then I read what happened to people who did.

One woman had someone build her store so she could get started quickly. When it was transferred to her, it was shut down almost immediately, and she wrote that she was in tears.

Another hired a freelancer, and soon after the store launched, "the nightmare began." A man paid two different experts and it still wasn't making sales.

Same chapter every time. Built, handed over, then nothing.

That night, around 1am, I went looking for why. I ended up in the platform's own guide for people who build stores for clients. It tells them to transfer ownership to the client "when it's ready to go live."

I read that line five times, and then every one of those posts made sense.

A store build is a project, and its end date is launch day. Nothing sneaky about it. It's the job description. The builder works on the store while it's closed, hands it over the moment it opens, and moves on to the next one.

But a store that isn't open can't tell anyone anything. Nobody has visited. No product has been tested. The first real information only starts arriving after it goes live: which products people click, which listings they leave, what a small ad test shows.

Every decision that shapes a new store runs on that information. Which product stays. Which one gets replaced. Which listing gets rewritten. What goes up next.

Think of a contractor who builds a restaurant and hands over the keys the night before opening. The building can be perfect. The first week is still when you find out which dishes people order and which ones come back to the kitchen.

And the contractor is long gone by then. He should be. That was never his job.

So the weeks right after launch are where a new store is made or lost, and that is exactly when the owner gets left alone. Those people didn't pick bad builders. They bought a job that ended on launch day.

I closed the tab. Fine, I thought. I'll finish it myself.

Week 10, Tuesday. Fourth theme image. Still not live. I drew the tenth tally mark on the sticky note stuck to the corner of my laptop, one for every Sunday I'd told myself this is the weekend it goes live. Then I put the laptop on the floor so I wouldn't have to look at it.

That's when it hit me. Even if I finished, I'd be standing alone in that restaurant on opening night, with nobody in the kitchen. Maybe the techies really are the only ones who understand this. No wonder people give up.

Week 10, Saturday. My nephew's seventh birthday. I was refilling the ice in my sister's kitchen when her neighbor came in for a lighter. My sister announced I'm opening an online store, and the neighbor asked when it goes live.

"Almost done," I said.

She laughed, not meanly. She'd paid someone to build hers last year. "Everybody warned me about the setup," she said. "The setup was the part he did. It was the week after that I needed somebody."

Then she said the thing I wrote on the back of my hand. "Next time, before I pay anyone, I'm asking one question. What do you do the week after it goes live?"

I had been asking the wrong question. First it was "how do I finish this setup," then "can I finish it myself." It was never either one. It was "who's still working on it after it goes live?"

Week 11, Monday. I typed her question into a search bar.

One page answered it as a list, which is the only way I trust anything anymore. It was on a site called Readymerce. For after the store goes live: an early performance review, post-launch corrections, ongoing listing optimisation and new product rollout. Products released in stages. Ad testing with budgets you approve.

I didn't trust it. I'd just read about people who paid for a store and got left holding it. And part of me still thought, what would stop me from just doing this myself?

Ten tally marks, that's what.

So I checked everything before paying a cent. The $500 is one time. Product costs, platform fees and ad spend are extra, and the page says so up front. The store is in my name and stays in my name. Payouts go to my own bank account.

There's even a line saying they make no income guarantees, which, weirdly, is what made me book the call.

On the call I asked what I'd been too embarrassed to ask anyone: is it something I have to run on my own? How much work they keep doing after launch gets agreed right there, with the platform and the scope. I wrote it all down.

I read the refund terms twice, too. Seven days from payment, on the $500 fee only, and it ends if you accept delivery, buy any add-on or ask for more work. At least it was in writing.

I paid. That night I closed the laptop before ten, and I stopped counting weeks.

The morning it went live, I opened it on my phone in the break room and looked at the owner field. My name. Mine, and it stays mine. I hadn't touched a single setting.

The first products weren't me flipping between candles and dog bandanas at midnight. They came from research on what people search for and how crowded it is, went up in stages, and each got a small ad test on a budget I approved between two patients.

Then the week after happened, with somebody in the kitchen.

The first written review came in. What to keep. What to replace. Which listing needed rewriting. What goes up next. The corrections got made. Nobody sent me a tutorial.

My sister opened the store on her phone at dinner, scrolled for a long time, and said, "Wait. This is actually yours?" She's stopped asking when it goes live.

It's Tuesday again, 9:40pm, and I'm not in the settings. The listings are up. Someone who isn't me is reading how they're doing and telling me what they'd change next. I approve what needs approving and close the laptop.

The sticky note with ten tally marks is in my desk drawer. I kept it on purpose.

If I could tell week-one me one thing: the setup was never the wall. It really is a maze, and being stuck in it said nothing about me.

But it's only the half that ends on launch day. The half that decides a store starts after, and without someone there, you get left on launch day.

What I needed was a store built in my name, products going live in stages, and people who stay after launch day. For me that started with the $500 Build.

Every week I spent in the settings was another week the store I started didn't exist. If there's a note on your screen counting weeks, ask the neighbor's question before you pay anyone.

There's a new note on my laptop now. Three words.

Live, not stuck.

story_hooks.text: Week 10, Tuesday, 9:40pm. I changed the theme image on my store again. That's the fourth one, and the store still isn't live.
A sticky note on my laptop has ten tally marks on it, one for every Sunday I swore my store would go live that weekend.
Everyone at work calls me when the computers act up. My own store has beaten me for ten weeks straight.
I haven't told anyone at work that I have an online store. It's been ten weeks, and it has never once been live.
Twenty-two help tabs open at 1am, and not one of them has gotten my store any closer to live.
